1. Read the three CSV files (NO2, Crime, neighbor‐list) into pandas DataFrames and clean the borough names so they match exactly across tables.  

2. Merge NO2 and Crime columns into a single DataFrame keyed on borough name.  

3. Handle missing data:  
   a. Drop any borough that is missing either its NO2_value or its Crime_value (pairwise listwise deletion).  
   b. Also remove these boroughs from every neighbor list so the spatial‐weights matrix only contains boroughs with complete data.  

4. Build the binary spatial‐weights matrix W (rows and columns ordered identically to the merged DataFrame):  
   • W_ij = 1 if j is listed as a neighbor of i, else 0;  
   • Set the diagonal to 0;  
   • Row‐standardize each row so the weights of each borough sum to 1.  

5. Compute Lee’s bivariate L statistic:  
   • Standardize both variables (z_NO2, z_Crime) to zero mean and unit variance.  
   • For each borough i, calculate the spatial lag of Crime: S_i = Σ_j W_ij * z_Crime_j.  
   • Lee’s L = (1/n) * Σ_i (z_NO2_i * S_i).  

6. Assess significance with a Monte-Carlo permutation test (≥500 permutations, e.g., 999):  
   • Randomly shuffle the Crime values among boroughs while keeping NO2 fixed; recompute L each shuffle.  
   • Build the reference distribution of L under the null hypothesis of spatial randomness.  
   • Two-sided p-value = proportion of shuffled L’s whose absolute value ≥ |observed L| (plus 1, divided by permutations+1).  

7. Interpret the result:  
   • If p < 0.05 and observed L > 0 → POSITIVE spatial association.  
   • If p < 0.05 and observed L < 0 → NEGATIVE spatial association.  
   • Otherwise → NOT SIGNIFICANT.  

8. Report the observed L (rounded to three decimals) and the p-value (rounded to three decimals) in the required format.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# 1. read data
data = pd.read_csv("chunks_csv/bivariate/bivariate_2021_no2_crime.csv")
adj  = pd.read_csv("chunks_csv/borough_adjacency.csv")

# 2. drop rows with missing NO2 or Crime
data_clean = data.dropna(subset=["NO2_value", "Crime_value"]).reset_index(drop=True)

# 3. build a set of valid boroughs and filter adjacency list
valid_boroughs = set(data_clean["borough"])
adj_clean = adj[adj["borough"].isin(valid_boroughs) & adj["neighbor"].isin(valid_boroughs)]

# 4. make an index mapping borough -> row number
index = {b:i for i,b in enumerate(data_clean["borough"])}
n = len(data_clean)

# 5. build weight matrix W (binary); then row-standardize
W = np.zeros((n, n), dtype=float)
for _, row in adj_clean.iterrows():
    i = index[row["borough"]]
    j = index[row["neighbor"]]
    W[i, j] = 1

# ensure diagonal = 0 (already) and row-standardize
row_sums = W.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
# avoid division by zero
row_sums[row_sums == 0] = 1
W = W / row_sums

# 6. standardize NO2 and Crime
z_no2   = (data_clean["NO2_value"]   - data_clean["NO2_value"].mean())   / data_clean["NO2_value"].std(ddof=0)
z_crime = (data_clean["Crime_value"] - data_clean["Crime_value"].mean()) / data_clean["Crime_value"].std(ddof=0)
z_no2   = z_no2.to_numpy()
z_crime = z_crime.to_numpy()

# spatial lag of crime
S = W.dot(z_crime)

# 7. Lee's L
L_obs = (z_no2 * S).mean()

# 8. permutation test
n_perm = 999
Ls = np.empty(n_perm)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
for k in range(n_perm):
    zc_perm = rng.permutation(z_crime)
    S_perm  = W.dot(zc_perm)
    Ls[k]   = (z_no2 * S_perm).mean()

# two-sided p-value
p = (np.sum(np.abs(Ls) >= abs(L_obs)) + 1) / (n_perm + 1)

# 9. verdict
if p < 0.05:
    verdict = "POSITIVE" if L_obs > 0 else "NEGATIVE"
else:
    verdict = "NOT SIGNIFICANT"

# 10. outputs
print(f"data_points_used = {n}")
print(f"FINAL ANSWER: {verdict} (test statistic = {L_obs}, p = {p})")
